Detailed Coaching Rationale & Programmin: Opens the cycle at 70% TM for 4x4, a volume/intensity combo you should be able to execute well short of failure. The job this week isn't to push RPE, it's to groove the pattern under load and establish a baseline your body can build on. Split squats and leg curls target the unilateral stability and hamstring strength that heavier squats will demand later.

Mirrors Day 1's approach at the same 70% TM. Close-grip bench and triceps work start building the lockout strength you won't need yet but will in Weeks 8-12. Face pulls are prophylactic — they keep the rear delts/rotator cuff balanced against all the pressing volume before it accumulates.

Deliberately the lightest relative-intensity day of the week (68% TM) because deadlift is the most fatigue-expensive lift you do — a 'moderate' deadlift session costs more recovery than a moderate squat or bench session. Paused deadlift and farmer's carries add extra pulling volume without loading the bar as heavy as the main lift, which is how you build deadlift work capacity without digging a hole this early.

This is a bench frequency day, not a second heavy bench day — the 3-1-1 tempo at 65% keeps intensity low while reinforcing bar path and control. The real work here is the back: rows and pulldowns build the upper-back tightness that stabilizes heavy bench press later, and this is the best week to start that development, before fatigue accumulates.

Primary Lifts Programmed: Paused squat / Rack pull baseline test
Detailed Coaching Rationale & Programmin: Paused squat adds positional strength work for the bottom of the squat. The rack pull test (working up to a clean RPE 8 top set) exists to establish your actual starting point for rack pull TM — everything for the next 12 weeks on that lift is calibrated off today's number, so treat it seriously but don't grind past RPE 8.

Same structure as Week 1, one set added (5x4) and intensity up 3% (73%). This is the standard accumulation progression — small, repeatable jumps that let you accumulate quality reps without a spike in fatigue.
Same logic as Day 1 — one more set, 3% more load. You should still be finishing sets with 2-3 reps in reserve.

Load moves to 72%, still 3 sets — deadlift is the one lift that doesn't get a set added here, because the fatigue cost per set is steep enough that stacking volume too fast is how deadlift-specific overreach happens. Paused deadlift intensity ticks up slightly to keep pace.

Paused bench replaces tempo bench as the frequency movement — it's a different stimulus (dead-stop strength off the chest) at the same intensity, which keeps this day from getting stale while still serving as a lower-stress second bench touch.

High bar squat at low intensity (65%) is a variation day — more quad emphasis, more upright torso, which builds a different piece of the squat than the low-bar/competition-style work on Day 1. Rack pull moves from a one-off test to real programmed work: 4x4 at 70%, mirroring the same volume approach as squat and bench.

Sets climb to 6x3 while reps per set drop — this is the volume peak of the block starting to show. Total load lifted keeps rising even though reps-per-set fall, which is how accumulation blocks build work capacity without needing RPE to spike.
Same pattern as squat — more sets, fewer reps, intensity now at 76%. RPE creeping to 7-8 is expected and fine; this is still sub-maximal work.
4x3 @ 76% — deadlift picks up a 4th set for the first time this cycle, timed for the middle of the block rather than the start, once your body has had two weeks to adapt to the lift's demands.

Spoto press (paused a few inches off the chest) targets the mid-range sticking point most lifters actually miss reps at — introducing it here, still light (60%), builds familiarity before it matters more in heavier weeks.
Tempo squat stays light and technical. Rack pull jumps to 5x3 @ 74% — the volume peak for that lift this week, same logic as squat and bench getting their heaviest work here.

6x3 @ 80% is the heaviest and most fatiguing squat session of the accumulation block — RPE 8 means you're finishing sets with genuine effort. This is the intended peak; next week is a deload specifically because this week is designed to leave you fatigued.
Same role as Day 1 — heaviest bench day of the block, RPE 8, 80% TM.

4x3 @ 80% is the heaviest deadlift session of the block. Notice the paused deadlift accessory disappears this week — deliberately, so total lower-back/grip fatigue doesn't stack on top of the heaviest main-lift day. Farmer's carries stay in since grip needs continuous exposure, but everything else backs off to let the main lift carry the load.

Volume on the accessories actually drops slightly this week (rows, pulldowns) — a quiet signal that fatigue is accumulating across the week and this day should feel like recovery relative to Monday and Tuesday, not another hard push.

Rack pull hits 5x3 @ 78%, its heaviest accumulation-block session. Coming the day after the week's other heavy work, this is the day fatigue is highest — RPE 8 here should feel harder than the same RPE 8 felt in Week 1.

Everything drops to 60% TM, RPE 6. The point of this week isn't to train — it's to let the four weeks of accumulated fatigue actually dissipate so Week 6 starts from a rested state. Resist the urge to push harder than prescribed; undermining the deload undermines the whole next block.
Same logic, same intensity drop.
Lightest deadlift session in the program (55% TM) — deadlift accumulates the most systemic fatigue of the three lifts, so it gets the biggest relative intensity drop during deload.
Volume across accessories is roughly half of Week 4 — this day should feel almost too easy. That's correct.
Both movements are explicitly 'easy' here — the goal is moving weight to keep the pattern fresh, not accumulating any new training stress.

Sets drop back to 5, reps stay at 3, but intensity jumps to 83% — the shift from accumulation logic (more volume, moderate intensity) to intensification logic (less volume, higher intensity) starts here. RPE 8 should feel similar to Week 4's RPE 8, even though the % is higher, because you're rested.
Same shift — 5x3 @ 83%, RPE 8.
3x3 @ 82% — deadlift volume actually drops (from 4 sets to 3) as intensity climbs, protecting recovery as the numbers on the bar get heavier.
Spoto press intensity ticks up modestly (65%) but stays a genuinely sub-maximal accessory day — this session's job is still support work, not pushing a new intensity high.
Rack pull moves to 4x3 @ 80%, matching the intensification shift seen everywhere else this week — fewer sets, heavier load.

Reps drop to 2, intensity to 87% — this is the point in the block where you should start feeling real weight on the bar. RPE 8 with 5 sets of 2 is a meaningfully different stimulus than Week 6's 5x3, even though the jump in % looks small.
Sets actually increase to 6x2 @ 87% — bench tends to tolerate slightly more frequency/volume at high intensity than squat or deadlift, which is why it gets an extra set here.
4x2 @ 86% — deadlift picks its set count back up now that intensity has stabilized into the doubles range, but stays a single weekly exposure.

Tempo bench returns as the frequency movement, still at a low, controlled intensity (65%) — this day's purpose hasn't changed all cycle: reinforce technique and support upper-back strength without adding to the week's fatigue total.
Rack pull climbs to 84% for 4x2 — tracking the same double-focused intensification pattern as the other three lifts.

4x2 @ 90%, RPE 8-9 — you're now within range of what a competition attempt will feel like. Set count drops to 4 as the weight gets heavy enough that quality on every rep matters more than total reps accumulated.
5x2 @ 90%, RPE 8-9 — same logic, same intensity.

3x2 @ 89%, RPE 8-9 — deadlift's lower set count here isn't a weakness in the program, it's intentional: this is the heaviest deadlift has been all cycle, and 3 quality doubles is enough stimulus without over-costing next week's recovery.
Accessory volume trims down further (2-3 sets across the board) — a sign the week's real work has already happened on Days 1-3 and this session exists to support, not add stress.
Rack pull hits 88% for 3x2, its heaviest point yet — matching deadlift and squat's approach to this stage of the block.

3x2 @ 90% with an optional single at 92% — this is the last near-max exposure before the taper begins, and it's deliberately capped rather than fixed. If your doubles feel fast and clean, the optional single gives you one true near-max data point; if they don't, skipping it protects the freshness you'll need in Weeks 11-13. This is the most important judgment call in the whole program — err toward skipping if in doubt.
Same structure — 4x2 @ 88% with an optional single @ 90%, gated by the same bar-speed rule.
2x2 @ 88% with an optional single @ 90% — deadlift's set count is intentionally lowest of the four lifts this week, since it recovers slowest and the taper is only two weeks away.
'Competition-style' means pause, grip, and setup exactly as you'll use on a platform — this is technical rehearsal at a manageable intensity (83%), not a new intensity push.
Rack pull follows the same optional-single structure as the main three lifts — 2x2 @ 86% with an optional single @ 88%, same bar-speed gate.

Back down to 65% TM, RPE 6 — this deload exists specifically to absorb whatever near-max singles you did take in Week 9. Even if you skipped every optional single, the four weeks of climbing intensity before it still need this reset.
Same intensity drop, same purpose.
60% TM — deadlift again gets the largest relative drop of the three lifts, consistent with every deload in this program.
Accessories are minimal here (2 sets max) — the only goal this session is blood flow and pattern maintenance.

Both movements explicitly 'easy' — by the end of this week you should feel noticeably fresher than you did entering it. If you don't, that's useful information: consider extending recovery before Week 11 rather than pushing into it fatigued.

A true heavy single at 90% TM, RPE 8-9 — deliberately lower than the original program's 92-93% call, because this is now two near-max exposures away from your actual PR attempt, not one. The back-off doubles at 82% add a small amount of extra quality volume without turning this into another intensification-style session.
Same structure and same reasoning — 90% single, back-off doubles at 82%.
A single heavy attempt at 88% and nothing else beyond reverse hyper — deadlift gets the least additional work of any lift this week because it has the least recovery runway left before test week.
Lower intensity (75%) than Week 9's version of this session — as you get closer to testing, every non-peak day should be getting easier, not staying flat.

Rack pull's 'heavy double, then stop' prescription at 87% (down from the original 90%) is the same taper logic applied to the fourth lift — protect the number you're chasing in Week 13 by not chasing a smaller number too close to it.

3x1 @ 85%, RPE 7-8, explicitly framed as 'crisp reps only, stop if speed drops.' This is the core taper principle: intensity stays moderate-high so the nervous system stays primed, but nothing here is a new max effort. The original program had a 95% single scheduled this week — the single biggest risk in the whole 13 weeks — and it's removed entirely.
Same taper logic — 3x1 @ 85%, speed-gated.
2x1 @ 82%, RPE 7 — deadlift's taper intensity is deliberately the lowest of the four lifts, since it has the least margin for error going into test week and recovers slowest of the four.
Purely maintenance — light lockout work and minimal accessory volume. Nothing in this session should register as hard.
Rack pull mirrors deadlift's approach — 2x1 @ 82%, RPE 7, a touch rather than a test.
Both squat and bench at 50% TM — just enough to prime the pattern and confirm everything feels normal. Nothing about this day should influence how heavy Monday's actual attempts feel.

Day Label / Focus: Day B — Bench PR (After 1 Rest Day)
Detailed Coaching Rationale & Programmin: First of the four PR attempts, placed earliest because bench recovers fastest of the four lifts — a good lift here doesn't cost you much for the squat attempt that follows.

Day Label / Focus: Day C — Squat PR (After 1 Rest Day)
Detailed Coaching Rationale & Programmin: Placed with a rest day of separation from bench, giving each lift its own attempt day rather than testing multiple lifts in one session, which is how fatigue from an early attempt quietly costs you a later one.

Day Label / Focus: Day D — Deadlift PR (After 2 Rest Days)
Detailed Coaching Rationale & Programmin: Given two full rest days beforehand — deadlift needs the most recovery of any lift in this program, and this is the day that recovery debt gets paid down before asking for a max effort.

Day Label / Focus: Day E — Rack Pull PR (After 2 Rest Days)
Detailed Coaching Rationale & Programmin: The last attempt in the program, and now separated from deadlift by two rest days instead of sitting on the very next training day as in the original layout. This single change — spacing the two pulling lifts apart — is the difference between rack pull's number reflecting your actual strength versus reflecting how tired your back was three days into a testing block.
